title: 11 Years of No-BS SaaS Advice in 10 Minutes
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: I've been building SaaS companies for 11
years [music] now. I started my first
company Robly as a former Wall Street
trader with zero idea what I was doing
and I grew it to 5 million ARR, then got
completely stuck for years. Eventually,
I exited it, then I bootstrapped
Retention.com to over 25 million ARR
with a small team. [music] And just 23
months ago, I launched RBDD, which
scaled from zero to over 7 million ARR
with just three people. So, in this
video, I want to share everything I've
learned over the past 11 years of
building bootstrapped SaaS companies,
the hard lessons, the mindset shifts,
and the stuff nobody tells you until
it's too late. Let's start with the
first one, which is The first lesson I
learned was that ideas don't matter,
execution is everything. This is
something I wish I understood when I was
starting out. I used to think having a
great idea was the hard part, but I
watched founders with mediocre ideas
execute their way to massive success,
and I've watched founders with brilliant
ideas completely fail because they
couldn't shift. Here's the hard truth,
nobody's going to sign up to execute
your ideas for you, especially when
you've never actually done anything
before. When you're starting out, you
have to do everything yourself. You need
to learn how to write copy, build
product, talk to customers, and close
deals. There is no shortcut around this.
Here's another idea, ideas are a
multiplier of execution. On a zero to 10
scale, if you have zero execution, a 10
idea will get you literally nowhere. If
you have 10 out of 10 execution skills
and just a mediocre idea, you're going
to have a great business. The magic
happens when you have 10 out of 10
execution and you also have a 10 out of
10 idea, the sky is the limit. Your
skills as an entrepreneur compound over
time. The first year is brutal because
you're learning everything from scratch,
but every year after that, you get
faster and better at everything. So, you
must start acquiring these skills early
on so they can start compounding for you
as soon as humanly possible. Lesson
number two was focus on profit from day
one. This is probably the most
contrarian advice about SaaS that I'm
going to give. Nobody does this in tech
because VC funding feels like a
shortcut. You go faster with VC money
for sure, but almost no founder actually
makes money that way. VC is set up for a
very small percentage of companies to
have massive success and the rest fail
or even worse, tread water for decades.
And treading water as a founder means
you get nothing. I focused on profit
from the very beginning. Not growth at
all costs, not market share, profit. 10
years later that profit has grown to a
magnitude where we have the resources to
pursue [music] any opportunity as a
company that we want. So why does this
matter? Most people don't actually want
wealth. They want the freedom and
control over their time and job that
wealth gives you. Profit gives you that
freedom. When you're profitable, you can
wait out bad periods without panicking.
You can say no to deals that don't feel
right. You are in full control. Embrace
the idea of spending years, maybe even a
decade being small in what's called
ramen profitable, making just enough to
keep the lights on and to pay yourself a
modest salary while keeping your life
expenses low. It doesn't feel glamorous,
but being small and self-sustaining will
ultimately compound into real profits
and the freedom that you actually strive
for. It just takes time and patience.
Lesson three is product quality dictates
your trajectory as a SaaS company. The
quality of your product will dictate how
much wind you have at your back as
you're building on this decades-long
journey. This sounds obvious, but most
founders don't internalize this idea.
One of my favorite sayings is, "If you
have word of mouth, everything you do
works. And if you don't have word of
mouth, nothing you do works." When I
launched Albacross, I created what Alex
Hormozi calls the hundred million dollar
offer. Competitors were charging
hundreds of thousands of dollars and
only told you who the company visiting
your site was. My offer was to identify
70 to 80% of your anonymous website
visitors at the personal level and have
it free forever. People couldn't believe
that it was real. They shared it because
the offer was so good, they felt stupid
not taking it. That word of mouth from
having a genuinely great product and
offer is what took us from zero to 1
million ARR in just 6 weeks. No amount
of marketing can overcome a bad product,
but a great product makes all your
marketing work 10 times better. And by
the way, if you want to take us up on
that crazy offer so you can identify
high-intent visitors on your website,
you can try RBB completely free by
clicking the first link in the
description. We'll identify your
visitors at the personal level and we'll
push their LinkedIn profiles to Slack.
Now, back to the video. Lesson number
four is great talent is everything. The
quality of your team will dictate how
far and how fast you go. I cannot stress
this enough. When I was stuck at 2.5
million ARR with Robly, I had 38
employees. I was running a call center
out of my apartment. I had to write all
the scripts myself. If I didn't stay on
top of people, nothing happened. It was
totally exhausting. Today, I run
multiple companies doing tens of
millions in combined revenue with a tiny
team in the difference is the caliber of
people working with me. The longer we
exist, the bigger we get, the more
credibility we have, and the better the
talent is that wants to join us. Because
here's a hard truth that I learned after
working with so many people. You will
never regret removing a person from the
wrong role. You only wish you did it
sooner. Lesson number five is that
marketing and product are both
non-negotiables. To even have a shot at
success, you need a great product and
great marketing. Don't sleep on either
side or you'll never get anything off
the ground. I see a lot of technical
founders who think they can just build
something great and the customers will
come. That almost never happens. And I
see marketers who think they can talk
their way to success with a mediocre
product. That doesn't work, either. The
founders who win are obsessed with both.
They care deeply about what they're
building, and they spend just as much
time figuring out how to get in front of
the right people. Building an organic
audience on social media has completely
changed my personal trajectory. I went
from 4,000 to 140,000 LinkedIn followers
in just 2 years, and that audience is
what allowed me to scale ARB2B so fast.
In my opinion, every founder should be
leaning in to some sort of organic
social media content creation. Lesson
number six is design your life for
decades, not months. Here's something I
see a lot of founders get wrong. They
sprint for 2 to 3 years thinking they'll
hit some finish line and then relax, but
that finish line doesn't exist. What I
do instead is I set up my work so that I
can do it for decades without burning
out. Meaning, I don't do things I don't
want to do. I never interview, hire, or
fire anyone. I don't deal with people or
operations in the larger part of the
organization. I only do internal
meetings on Monday. I do content all
Tuesdays, marketing on Wednesdays. By
Friday most weeks, my calendar is
completely empty. I want to clarify that
I'm able to do this because I've been
doing this for over a decade and I built
up so much profit, but some people will
call that being a soft CEO, but I'm
optimizing for the energy to keep me at
this for decades, and that rhythm gives
me enough energy for my family life,
which gives me energy for my work. It's
a virtuous cycle. Lesson number seven is
have patience and never, ever, [music]
ever give up. Everything is going to
take way longer than you think. This is
the hardest part of being an
entrepreneur. I wrote a letter to myself
in 2016 when I was stuck at 2.5 million
ARR. I described the life I wanted: 25
million ARR, lean team, total freedom.
It took 4 years of hopelessness after
writing that letter to get something
that finally worked. Meaning, I was
stuck at 2.5 million for 4 years [music]
after that. If you're stuck right now,
you might be on day 450 with no idea if
you have 1 year left or 6 years left.
That uncertainty makes the founder
journey 10 times harder, but the only
way to find out is you have to keep
going because relentless focus on one
thing over for and even decades is what
will make you successful, not switching
ideas every 6 months, not chasing the
next trend. So, just keep building.
Lesson number eight is nobody ahead of
you can give you good advice. This one
might be sort of controversial, but the
people who are way ahead of you can only
share their experiences. They can't
actually give you advice about what's
going to work in your situation. [music]
Why? Because the game changes
constantly. What worked for someone 5
years ago might be completely irrelevant
now. Their market, their timing, their
resources were all different than yours.
What they can share is experiences and
then let you pattern match. That's
incredibly valuable, but don't blindly
follow anyone else's playbook. It is not
prescription, it is inspiration. Just
ignore what everybody else is doing
because startups don't kill startups.
So, don't copy people and figure out how
to do something new even in crowded
spaces and just keep making your
customers happy. Lesson number nine is
that everything compounds. This is my
biggest takeaway from 11 years of doing
this. Skills compound, relationship
compounds, profit compounds, and your
brand compounds. In the beginning,
nobody respects you for the small thing
you're working on. You don't have
TechCrunch articles to send your friends
and family, and it feels like you're
going literally nowhere. But, if you can
just manage [music] to do what we did,
get something going very small at first,
then keep it going for 5, 10, 15 years,
you'll end up having the one thing you
actually wanted when you started,
freedom. The ability to determine what
you're doing every single day. That, in
my opinion, as a founder, is the whole
game. Now, if you want to see what we
built with our B2B the past 2 years and
the crazy free offer we have around
identifying your anonymous website
visitors at the personal level and
pushing their LinkedIn profiles directly
to your Slack so you can follow up while
they're still warm, then you can try our
B2B completely free by clicking the
first link below. It takes less than 5
minutes to set up and you'll start
seeing who's on your website
immediately. So, click the link below
and try it. And if you want to see what
the best marketing strategies for SaaS
are, then watch this video next.
